header:
Date: 2027-09-20
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Silva (Redwood SE), Alex Gomez (CTO - Cerulean), Maya Chen (ML Engineer - Cerulean), Samir Patel (Infra Lead - Cerulean)
summary: Technical deep-dive into KV-cache architecture, observed evictions during long-context flows, paging behavior, and prefix reuse patterns. Discussed tradeoffs (latency vs memory), eviction heuristics, quantization impact, and options for VPC/on-prem deployment sizing. Agreed to run targeted eviction benchmarks and share logs and security docs.
topics: Quantization impact on memory and performance
VPC / on-prem sizing and KMS concerns
transcript:
[00:00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're doing a KV-cache architecture deep-dive with Cerulean — Marco and I from Redwood, and the Cerulean folks. Quick intros?
[00:00:12] Alex Gomez: Yeah, Alex here, CTO. Maya is our ML engineer, Samir handles infra. Thanks for making time.
[00:00:20] Marco Silva: Cool. High level, we wanted to dig into the evictions you've been seeing and try to reproduce. We saw the notes you sent about long-context jobs hitting evictions around 30k tokens.
[00:00:35] Maya Chen: Correct. With our LLM pipelines, we often keep long prefix contexts — conversation history plus doc context — and the cache seems to flush, then tail latency spikes.
[00:00:46] Samir Patel: Right, and sometimes we see paging activity on the host, which is odd because we configured 240GB per GPU instance.
[00:00:55] Marco Silva: Mm-hm. A couple of quick clarifying Qs: are you using Dedicated or private on-prem today? And are you running mixed precision quantized weights?
[00:01:05] Alex Gomez: We're on Dedicated with Redwood, but evaluating private VPC next quarter. Models are 4-bit quantized for cost, and we do mixed batches — short user queries and long context QA jobs.
[00:01:18] Lena Park: Got it. That mix is key — the runtime tries to optimize kernel selection and KV cache policy, but heterogeneous sequence lengths and quantization interplay can cause memory layout inefficiencies.
[00:01:30] Maya Chen: Can you explain how prefix reuse affects eviction? We expect repeated prefixes to keep hot entries in cache, but we still see evictions for reused prefixes.
[00:01:41] Marco Silva: Sure. So our KV cache uses a per-shard LRU with windowed reference counting. If a prefix is reused but the working set exceeds the allocated KV pages, older entries get evicted even if logically hot. There's also a paging threshold — when mem exceeds X% we start reclaiming pages. In practice, small differences in tokenization or role tokens create slightly different prefix keys, hurting reuse.
[00:02:05] Alex Gomez: Ah, yes, we do sometimes have subtle tokenization changes between the user prompt and the evaluation harness. That's probably causing near-duplicates.
[00:02:15] Lena Park: That matches what we see. Also quantization can slightly change KV sizes; 4-bit quant profiles sometimes enlarge intermediate buffers depending on kernel. So even if the model memory footprint looks smaller, the runtime's staging buffers can push you over the paging threshold.
[00:02:29] Samir Patel: We're seeing the OS start swapping the page cache — that was my concern. Is there a recommended overprovisioning factor? We gave 240GB but maybe need more.
[00:02:40] Marco Silva: For long-context heavy workloads, we typically recommend at least 1.25x working set overhead for KV pages plus buffer headroom. So if your observed peak KV size is 180GB, target 225GB available to runtime. If you're on Dedicated, we can reserve larger GPUs or pin model shards to avoid cross-host paging.
[00:02:56] Maya Chen: When you say pin shards, is that in Dedicated or would that also help in VPC on-prem?
[00:03:04] Marco Silva: Both. Pinning avoids remote fetch penalties and reduces cross-host eviction churn. On-prem you have more control — we can recommend numa bindings and hugepage settings.
[00:03:15] Alex Gomez: How about the eviction policy itself? Is it LRU only or context-aware?
[00:03:21] Marco Silva: It's LRU with heuristics — we do weighted recency: larger prefixes get a bigger eviction cost so many small high-frequency entries don't evict a few large long-context entries immediately. But with prefix reuse misalignment, you still get churn.
[00:03:35] Lena Park: Also we have a mode that prioritizes prefix roots for streaming chat use-cases — that helps when you keep adding new turns but reuse the earlier context heavily. We can toggle that for your workload.
[00:03:47] Maya Chen: Is there any telemetry we can provide to help tune policies?
[00:03:52] Marco Silva: Yes. If you can share sample request traces with token counts, timestamps, and the observed evictions (our SDK can log hit/miss per request), we can run an offline simulation. Samir, you mentioned paging logs — those OS dmesg/sar logs are helpful too.
[00:04:07] Samir Patel: We'll pull the last 48h traces and dmesg. One more — prefix reuse: could canonicalizing prompts or deduping help?
[00:04:16] Lena Park: Absolutely. Canonicalizing role tokens and stable tokenization gives much better reuse. Small variations like a trailing space or punctuation often flip the tokenizer. We recommend a lightweight normalization layer pre-tokenize.
[00:04:29] Alex Gomez: Sounds doable. What about batching — we batch a lot for throughput; does that worsen eviction?
[00:04:36] Marco Silva: Batching can actually help amortize kernel overhead, but if batch construction interleaves very long and very short sequences, it increases the runtime's internal buffer peaks. We suggest bucketing by sequence length and using dynamic batching windows tuned for your latency SLOs.
[00:04:52] Maya Chen: We saw a scenario where a 40k token request arrived in a batch with many short requests and everything tripped memory. We thought the runtime would signal backpressure.
[00:05:01] Marco Silva: It does, but backpressure is configurable and sometimes disabled for max throughput. We can enable stricter admission control for long requests so they either get dedicated slots or are scheduled alone.
[00:05:12] Alex Gomez: Can quantization cause more frequent cache evictions?
[00:05:16] Marco Silva: Indirectly. Quantization changes memory layout and sometimes requires extra staging buffers for certain GPU kernels. Also some 4-bit kernels break large KV into more fragments, increasing bookkeeping overhead. We have quant-profile recommendations per model; we'll share those.
[00:05:29] Lena Park: I'll attach the model/quantization guidance doc. For your fleet, Marco recommended running a comparative test: same workload with 4-bit vs 8-bit profiles and measure hit rates and paging.
[00:05:40] Maya Chen: Ok. Regarding VPC/on-prem — are there restrictions on KMS usage or audit logs that we should be aware of?
[00:05:46] Lena Park: For Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. We can support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and bring-your-own-HSM for on-prem. Audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; we keep token-level anonymized traces on request under enterprise agreements.
[00:05:59] Samir Patel: Good. For on-prem we'll need guidance on NUMA, NIC tuning, and GPU interconnects — any docs?
[00:06:06] Marco Silva: Yes — we have an infra playbook for on-prem sizing with explicit hugepage, rmem/wmem, and NVLink recommendations. I'll share the link. Also recommend disabling swap entirely for inference hosts.
[00:06:17] Alex Gomez: Disabling swap — noted. We've seen OOM killer in dev; want to avoid production flakiness.
[00:06:23] Lena Park: Quick aside — we sometimes saw misattributed speaker labels in the logs; the transcript tool shows slightly garbled model names earlier in your initial notes. Sorry if that confused things.
[00:06:32] Maya Chen: No worries. Back to eviction: is there a way to persist hot prefixes to disk to avoid recompute when evicted?
[00:06:40] Marco Silva: We experimented with persistent cache tiers — store serialized KV pages on fast NVMe as a second-level cache. It reduces recompute but adds I/O latency on cold loads. For heavy long-context workloads, a hybrid approach helps: keep hot prefixes in RAM, slightly less hot on NVMe. That's the paging we referenced earlier — but it's better controlled than OS swapping.
[00:06:57] Samir Patel: So NVMe tier is better than swap. Makes sense. Any operational cost implications?
[00:07:03] Marco Silva: Yes, more provisioned NVMe and IOPS costs; but it's predictable compared to unbounded OS swapping. We can model cost vs tail-latency tradeoffs in the benchmark.
[00:07:12] Alex Gomez: Can Redwood's routing help — like route long-context to a different capacity pool?
[00:07:17] Lena Park: Yes, smart routing is a strong lever. Route long-context/low QPS infrequent jobs to larger-memory nodes and keep short low-latency traffic on smaller, cheaper nodes. That reduces eviction churn.
[00:07:27] Maya Chen: If we route, will there be cold start penalties when switching pools?
[00:07:31] Marco Silva: Slightly, but we can pre-warm. Also with Dedicated we can reserve a small warm pool to avoid cold misses.
[00:07:39] Alex Gomez: Would automatic prefix canonicalization be something Redwood can do in the runtime?
[00:07:44] Marco Silva: We could add optional normalization hooks pre-tokenize; it's non-trivial but doable. For now, doing it at your client layer is fastest.
[00:07:52] Samir Patel: Regarding metrics — what dashboards should we send?
[00:07:55] Lena Park: Send per-request token counts, cache hit/miss counts, mem usage over time, tail latency p95/p99, and any page fault counters. We'll ingest and simulate.
[00:08:05] Maya Chen: We'll export a 24-48h window and anonymize IDs.
[00:08:09] Marco Silva: Great. For benchmarking, I'll run two experiments: 1) reproduce with your traces against our staging with current eviction parameters; 2) run the NVMe tier sim and a 4-bit vs 8-bit quant compare.
[00:08:21] Alex Gomez: Timeline?
[00:08:23] Marco Silva: Benchmark 1 by 2027-09-27, results and suggested config by 2027-09-29.
[00:08:29] Lena Park: Action items summarized — we'll email the doc links and schedule the VPC sizing call. Any final Qs?
[00:08:36] Maya Chen: One — do you have a recommended admission control config for our current latency SLO of 150ms p95 on short queries?
[00:08:43] Marco Silva: Yes — configure two queues: low-latency lane (short sequences, max batch size 8, deadline scheduling) and high-memory lane (allow single large requests or small batches). We'll provide exact knobs in the config doc.
[00:08:56] Samir Patel: Sounds good. We'll also sanity-check kernel selection flags in current deploy.
[00:09:01] Alex Gomez: Thanks, everyone.
[00:09:04] Lena Park: Thanks — we'll follow up with the links and benchmark plan.
[00:09:08] [End of recording — remaining 46 minutes of technical discussion and Q/A omitted from this export as per storage settings, but core next steps captured above.]
